3. The defendant No. 1 the vendor who is since dead, the predecessor of the appellant before us, contested the suit. Other defendants, namely, defendant Nos. 2 to 6,7,8,9 and 11 filed written statement but ultimately they did not contest the suit. They had no independent claim in the suit land as they claimed to be the borgadars. The defendant No. 1 substituted by defendant No, 1 (Ka) to 1 (Gha) took several objections, the principal one being that the suit was barred by limitation. The suit was once tried by the court of first instance which disposed of the suit only on the question of limitation alone. On appeal the judgment was set aside and the suit was remanded for trial on all the issues involved therein. On remand the trial court decreed the suit and found that the suit was not barred by limitation. The defendants again preferred an appeal against the decision of trial court. The learned Court of appeal below affirmed the judgment of the trial court and found that the suit was not barred by law of limitation. This appeal is directed against the aforesaid decision of the learned Court of appeal below affirming that of the trial court. 

 5. The contract upon which the present suit was filed was dated 23-5-53 and the suit was filed on 3-2-59 which was beyond 3 years from the date of contract. The plaintiff claimed computation of the period of limitation under section 14 of the Limitation Act i.e. the plaintiff claim exclusion of the time during which the plaintiff had been prosecuting with diligence another suit. It is necessary in this connection to reproduce the provision of section 14 of the Limitation Act which is as follows:- 

 "14. Exclusion of time of proceeding bonafide in Court without jurisdiction :- (1) In computing the period of limitation for any suit the time during which the plaintiff has been prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding whether in a court of first instance or of appeal or revision, against the same party for the same relief shall be excluded, where the proceeding relates to the same matter in issue and is prosecuted in good faith in a court which, from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it, 

 (2) In computing the period of limitation for any application, the time during which the applicant has been prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding, whether in a court of first instance or of appeal or revision, against the same party for the same relief shall be excluded, where such proceeding is prosecuted in good faith in a court which, from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature is unable to entertain in," 

 6. Let the facts which are not in dispute and upon which the plaintiff claims exclusion of the time taken in the earlier proceeding under section 14 of the Limitation Act be stated shortly. One Rajani Mohan Roy, the predecessor of defendant Nos. 2 to 6 instituted a suit in the trial court on 28-5-52 for specific performance of contract against the defendant No. 1, the vendor and the plaintiff and his brother with respect to the self same land. The suit was decreed on 31-3-54. The plaintiff and his brother who contested the suit being being aggrieved by the decision filed an appeal against the aforesaid judgment of the trial court. The appeal was once allowed on 24.4.57 but before the hearing the respondent died and hence the appeal was again heard on substitution of the heirs after setting aside the abatement and on 31.5,58 the appeal was allowed. The plaintiff-respondent has submitted that the period between 28.5.52 and 31.5.58 should be excluded from the period of limitation of this suit because his right to sue against the present defendants was suspended during pendency of the earlier suit. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the court of appeal below erred in law in holding that the period of limitation from 28.5.52 to 31.5.58 remained suspended by reason of the pendency of title Suit No. 104 of 1932 and the connected Title Appeal No. 128 of 1954. He has further submitted that the court of appeal below and in law in not holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to exclusion of time under section 14 of the Limitation Act inasmuch as the legal requirements of section 14 of the Limitation Act are not present in the facts and circumstances of the case. In support of his submissions he has referred to me the decision in the case of Dwijeadra Narayan Roy v. Joges Chandra De and others (1) ; Abdus Sattar Chowdhury and erasers v. Abdul Rusan and others (2) ; Gaya Prasad v. Ram Setup (3) : Karsondas Dhunjibhoy v, Surajbhan Ramrijpal and others (4) ; Ramakrishna Chettair & others v. layarama Ives end others (5) Part Canning & land Improvement Co. Ltd. v. Achhiruddin Molla and others (6) Mr. B. B. Roy Chowdhury the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the plaintiff respondent relied upon the decision referred to in the court of appeal below as well as on the cases of Madhavdas ParmaImola v. Jan Mohammad Ghulam Hyder (7) Dwijendra Nrayan Roy v. loges Chandra be & ors (1) and Ramdutta Ratnitissendass v. E.D. Sassoon & Co. (8) 

 7. Section 14 of the Limitation Act does not prescribe any period of limitation but provides a method of calculation for excluding the period during which the plaintiff prosecuted with diligence another civil proceeding founded upon the same cause of action but proceeding failed for defect of jurisdiction or for other like defect. The essentials for application of section 14 of the Limitation Act are that the cause of action in both the proceedings should be same, the plaintiff must have prosecuted the earlier proceeding its good faith and that the earlier suit failed for absence of jurisdiction or for like defect. On the question as to whether it is necessary that the plaintiff of the later suit must have been prosecuting the earlier suit as a plaintiff, we are of opinion that it is not necessary that the plaintiff of the later suit should be prosecuting the earlier suit as a plaintiff. He is entitled to exclusion of the period during which the earlier suit was pending and in which he as a defendant urged the same claim as he afterwards preferred as plaintiff. Reliance for this view may be placed in the cases of Madhavdas Parmanand v. Jan Mohammad Ghulam Hyder (9) and in the case of Srimati Nrityamen Dassi and others v. Lakhan Chunder Son (since deseased) and others. (10) Though I am of the view that a defendant is also entitled to the benefit of section 14 yet the cause of action of the plaintiff in the earlier suit should be the same as in the later suit. In the case reported in 20 C.W.N. (P.C.) 522 where the defendant was found to be entitled to the benefit of section 14 of the Limitation Act, the prayer of the plaintiff in earlier suit also included the relief in favour of defendant who was a co-sharer of the plaintiff. In that view, the later suit by the defendant, after dismissal of the earlier suit because the earlier suit was for ejectment and not for partition, was held to be within time after exclusion of the period during which the earlier suit was pending. Let us now consider whether the cause of action of both the proceedings is the same or whether the previous proceeding was founded on the same cause of action. "Cause of action" means the whole of the material facts which is necessary for the plaintiff to allege and prove in order to succeed and creates the foundation for the suit. Cause of action is synonymous with the right to sue. It has not relation to the defence that may be set up. 

 8. The cause of action of the suit filed by the Rajani Mohan Roy, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 2 to 6 was founded upon his alleged contract to purchase the suit land with the defendant No. 1 the vendor. His cause of action was in our opinion distinct and was based upon certain facts independent of the facts upon which the plaintiff based his claim in subsequent suit. The plaintiff based his subsequent suit on the basis of his own contract. The plaintiff as codefendant in the earlier suit in defence though constituted his cause of action in the later suit, it cannot be said that the facts averred in defence constituted a cause of action of the suit instituted by Rajani Mohan Roy. We are of opinion that though the subject matter of both the suits were the same property, causes of action are not the same but different and independent of the other. It is seen that plaintiff could not obtain the relief he was entitled to in the earlier suit when resisting the claim of Rajani Mohan on the basis of his baina. It has been argued by the learned Advocate on behalf of the plaintiff respondent that even if a suit was filed by the plaintiff within the period prescribed, that suit could not be proceeded with in view of the provisions of section 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. So, it appears to us that the submission of the learned Advocate is based on the reasons that when the matter in issue in both the suits are the same the plaintiff of the later suit is entitled to exclusion of time under section 14 of the Limitation Act. Matters in issue in both the suits may be the same but cause of action and matter in issue are not synonymous. The term 'matter in issue" is wide in scope and in fact law in India as envisaged in section 14 of the Limitation Act has been amended by substituting the words "cause of action" with the words 'matter in issue' to enable a wider application of section 14 of the Limitation Act. As regards prosecution of earlier suit as a defendant in good faith, we are of opinion that in the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that the plaintiff was prosecuting the earlier case with the knowledge that he would get his relief under his contract in that suit but he was resisting the claim of another claimant in the property. It should, therefore, be held that the plaintiff did not file the later suit within time under an ill advice. 

 9. Another requirement of application of section 14 of the Limitation Act is that the earlier suit failed on the ground of absence of jurisdiction of the court or for other causes of like matter. In the present case, the suit was not dismissed for want of jurisdiction or for defect of like nature. The suit was dismissed on appeal not on the ground of want of jurisdiction but on merits of the case. The decision referred to in the judgment of the Court of appeal below, namely, 39 C.L.J. 40 did not consider the scope of applicability of the Limitation Act. The question that arose in the decision was the applicability of the principle of res judicata does not support the case of the plaintiff. The cause of action occurs only when the aggrieved parties right to apply to the proper trial. In the present case cause of action for the plaintiff appellant for institution of the later suit arose when the vendor i.e. the defendant No. 1 at the earlier suit by his written statement denied the contract with the present plaintiff. We are of the view that the earlier suit was an independent litigation and the time spent in prosecuting that litigation cannot be excluded from time prescribed under law to enforce this contract. We do not find any applicability of section 14 of the Limitation Act in the present suit since cause of action for the later suit was distinct from that of the earlier one. In view of discussion above I find substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant.
